overview.title: REST API hosting choices and deploying a model on a device
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: Finishing the REST-API deployment option (self-hosted vs. managed cloud) and introducing on-device deployment: when to use it and which tools (export(), TensorFlow Lite, ONNX runtime) make it possible.
overview.central_idea: Where a model runs is an engineering decision driven by connectivity, latency, data sensitivity, and device resources. A REST API suits most of the chapter's example projects, but when latency, offline use or privacy dominate, the model must run on the device itself, usually as a smaller, slightly less accurate model exported via `export()` to TensorFlow Lite or ONNX.
overview.importance: This page turns the abstract constraints gathered in section 6.1 (end-to-end encryption for the spam filter, factory latency for the cookie detector) into concrete deployment decisions. It teaches the decision criteria that practitioners actually use when choosing between server-side and edge inference.
learning_objectives: Identify which of the chapter's example projects are well served by a REST API, and why
Weigh self-hosting a model server against a fully managed cloud service such as Cloud AI Platform
List the four conditions under which on-device deployment is the right choice
Explain the efficiency-vs-accuracy tradeoff imposed by memory and power constraints
Name the tools Keras offers for on-device deployment: export() to a TensorFlow or ONNX save, TensorFlow Lite, ONNX runtime
prerequisites: The idea of an inference model distinct from the training-time Python object (p.208)
REST API deployment with TensorFlow Serving and ONNX and its usage conditions (p.209)
The chapter's running example projects and their constraints (p.196, p.197)
Compilation of a model into a computation graph (chapter 3)

paragraphs.excerpt: For instance, the image search engine project, the music recommender system,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Four of the chapter's example projects (image search, music recommendation, credit card fraud detection, satellite imagery) are good candidates for REST API serving.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These projects meet the conditions from the previous page. Their consumers have reliable internet access, a round trip of about 500 ms is acceptable, and the inputs are not so sensitive that they cannot be decrypted on a server. Fraud checks and recommendations happen on the company's own servers, and satellite imagery analysis is offline batch-style work.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It grounds the abstract checklist in concrete cases and shows that REST serving is the default for most server-side ML products.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The deployment target follows from the constraints identified while framing the problem (section 6.1).

terminology.meaning: An HTTP interface where a client sends a request (e.g., JSON input) to a server endpoint and receives the model's prediction in the response.

connections: p.209: the three conditions for REST deployment (connectivity, no strict latency, non-sensitive data)
p.196: the list of example projects introduced at the start of chapter 6

paragraphs.excerpt: An important question when deploying a model as a REST API is
paragraphs.what_it_says: When serving via REST you must choose between hosting the serving code yourself and using a fully managed cloud service. Google's Cloud AI Platform lets you upload a TensorFlow model to GCS and get an API endpoint, and it handles batching, load balancing and scaling.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Self-hosting (e.g., running TensorFlow Serving on your own machines) gives control but makes you responsible for operations. A managed service takes on the operational work: grouping incoming requests into batches for efficient hardware use, spreading traffic across replicas, and adding or removing capacity as demand changes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Much of the cost of production ML is operational. Knowing that managed options exist helps a team decide whether to build serving infrastructure or buy it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Batching predictions works because accelerators process a batch of N inputs in roughly the time of a few single inputs. Servers therefore hold requests for a few milliseconds to form batches (beyond the book).

terminology.meaning: A cloud product where the provider runs and maintains the infrastructure; you supply only the model.
Google's object storage service, used here as the place where the saved model is uploaded.
Distributing incoming requests across several server instances so none is overloaded.
Adjusting the number of serving instances to match request volume.

connections: p.209: TensorFlow Serving and ONNX export via export()
p.580: GCS also appears as a data source for TPU training

paragraphs.excerpt: Sometimes, you may need your model to live on the same device
paragraphs.what_it_says: Some models must run on the same device as the application that uses them: a smartphone, an embedded ARM CPU on a robot, or a microcontroller. Cameras that detect people and faces probably run a small deep learning model on board.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is often called edge inference: no network hop, with the computation happening where the data is produced. The devices range from powerful (phones with neural accelerators) to tiny (microcontrollers with kilobytes of RAM).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces a deployment target with constraints very different from a server's, and these constraints shape model design.

terminology.meaning: A low-power processor based on the ARM architecture, common in robots, phones and IoT hardware.
A very small computer on a single chip, with tight memory (often kilobytes to a few MB) and power budgets.

connections: p.208: production environments may not support Python at all, e.g., embedded systems

paragraphs.excerpt: Your model has strict latency constraints or needs to run in
paragraphs.what_it_says: First condition: strict latency or low connectivity. For immersive augmented reality, querying a remote server is not viable.
paragraphs.what_it_means: AR must react within a single display frame (tens of milliseconds). A REST round trip of about 500 ms (p.209), or no connection at all, rules out server inference.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the mirror image of the first two REST conditions. Device deployment is chosen when those conditions fail.

terminology.meaning: Time between providing an input and receiving the prediction.

connections: p.209: REST round trip typically takes around 500 ms

paragraphs.excerpt: Your model can be made sufficiently small that it can run
paragraphs.what_it_says: Second condition: the model can be made small enough to fit the device's memory and power constraints.
paragraphs.what_it_means: On-device deployment is only an option if a compact model can do the job. Typical tools are smaller architectures, weight quantization and pruning (beyond the book on this page).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a feasibility check. Some models, such as large generative models, cannot run on small devices.

terminology.meaning: The energy budget of a battery-powered or low-power device, which limits how much computation can run.

connections: p.208: inference-only models leave room for optimizations that reduce memory footprint

paragraphs.excerpt: Getting the highest possible accuracy isn’t mission critical for your task: there
paragraphs.what_it_says: Third condition: top accuracy is not mission critical, because runtime efficiency and accuracy trade off. Device constraints often force you to ship a model weaker than the best one you could run on a large GPU.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Shrinking a model usually costs some accuracy. You have to accept that the shipped model sits at a different point on the efficiency/accuracy curve than your best research model.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets expectations with stakeholders (section 6.3.1). The deployed on-device model will usually be somewhat worse than the validation numbers of the largest model.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Efficiency–accuracy Pareto frontier: for a fixed task, more parameters and compute generally buy accuracy up to a point.

terminology.meaning: How fast and with how little memory/energy a model computes a prediction.

paragraphs.excerpt: The input data is strictly sensitive and thus shouldn’t be decryptable
paragraphs.what_it_says: Fourth condition: the input data is strictly sensitive and must not be decryptable on a remote server.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A server-side model must see plaintext inputs. If even the service provider is not allowed to read the data, the model has to come to the data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Privacy can be a hard requirement that decides the architecture regardless of cost.

terminology.meaning: Able to be turned back into readable plaintext; with end-to-end encryption only the endpoints hold the keys.

connections: p.209: REST serving requires data to be available on the server in decrypted form

paragraphs.excerpt: For instance, our spam detection model will need to run on
paragraphs.what_it_says: The spam detection model must run on the user's smartphone because messages are end-to-end encrypted and cannot be read by a remote model. The bad-cookie detector has strict latency constraints and must run at the factory, but with no power or space constraints it can use a GPU.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two projects reach device deployment for different reasons: privacy for spam filtering, latency for cookie detection. The factory case shows that "on device" does not always mean tiny hardware. It can be a local GPU machine next to the conveyor belt.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It completes the story begun in section 6.1, where these constraints were first uncovered, and shows how they determine deployment.

terminology.meaning: Encryption where only sender and recipient can decrypt messages; intermediate servers see only ciphertext.

connections: p.197: constraints identified while framing the problem: encrypted chat app, cookie-filter latency

paragraphs.excerpt: To deploy a Keras model on a smartphone or embedded device, you
paragraphs.what_it_says: Use `export()` again to create a TensorFlow or ONNX save that includes the computation graph. TensorFlow Lite is a framework for efficient on-device inference on Android, iOS, ARM CPUs, Raspberry Pi and some microcontrollers, and it uses the same saved-model format as TensorFlow Serving. The ONNX runtime also runs on mobile.
paragraphs.what_it_means: One export mechanism feeds several runtimes. The exported artifact (weights plus graph, independent of Python) can be served by TensorFlow Serving on a server or converted and run by TensorFlow Lite on a phone.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Keras users do not need to rewrite models for each platform. The work is in choosing the runtime and fitting the constraints.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in practice a SavedModel is usually passed through the TFLite converter to produce a `.tflite` flatbuffer, often with quantization, before it is put on a device.

terminology.meaning: TensorFlow's lightweight inference runtime for mobile and embedded devices (since rebranded by Google as LiteRT).
A cross-platform inference engine for models in the Open Neural Network Exchange format.
The model's operations recorded as a static graph that can execute without the Python program.

concepts.name: REST API model serving
concepts.definition: Exposing a trained model through an HTTP endpoint that clients query for predictions.
concepts.intuition: The model lives on your server; apps send it inputs and get answers back.
concepts.technical: Served via TensorFlow Serving or ONNX after `export()`; can be self-hosted or managed (e.g., Cloud AI Platform), which handles batching, load balancing and scaling.
concepts.significance: The simplest way to turn a model into a product when connectivity, latency and privacy allow it.
concepts.example: The credit card fraud detection project, scoring transactions on the company's servers.
concepts.misconception: That REST serving is always best. It fails for offline, low-latency or privacy-critical use.

concepts.name: Managed cloud model serving
concepts.definition: A third-party cloud service that hosts your uploaded model and provides an API endpoint.
concepts.intuition: Renting a fully staffed serving facility instead of building your own.
concepts.technical: With Cloud AI Platform you upload a TensorFlow model to GCS; the platform handles batching predictions, load balancing and scaling.
concepts.significance: Removes most operational burden from small teams.
concepts.example: Uploading the music recommender model to GCS and calling the endpoint from the radio app.
concepts.misconception: That managed means free of tradeoffs. You give up control and accept vendor lock-in and cost (inference, not in the book).

concepts.name: On-device (edge) deployment
concepts.definition: Running the model on the same device as the application: phone, embedded CPU, microcontroller, or local machine.
concepts.intuition: Bring the model to the data instead of the data to the model.
concepts.technical: Chosen when latency or connectivity is critical, the model can be made small enough, peak accuracy isn't mission critical, or data must not be decrypted remotely. Implemented with `export()` plus TensorFlow Lite or the ONNX runtime.
concepts.example: The spam filter running inside an end-to-end encrypted chat app on the phone.
concepts.misconception: That on-device always means low-power hardware. The cookie detector runs on a GPU at the factory.

concepts.name: Efficiency–accuracy tradeoff
concepts.definition: Smaller, faster models generally achieve lower accuracy than the best large models.
concepts.intuition: A pocket dictionary is handier but less complete than an unabridged one.
concepts.technical: Memory and power limits force a choice of model size; the shipped model is often not as good as what a large GPU could run.
concepts.significance: Must be communicated when setting expectations for device-deployed models.
concepts.example: A compressed face-detection model on a camera missing some small faces a server model would catch.
concepts.misconception: That compression is free. Some accuracy is usually lost.

concepts.name: TensorFlow Lite
concepts.definition: A framework for efficient on-device deep learning inference.
concepts.intuition: A slimmed-down TensorFlow engine that fits on phones and boards.
concepts.technical: Runs on Android, iOS, ARM CPUs, Raspberry Pi and certain microcontrollers; uses the same TensorFlow saved-model format as TensorFlow Serving.
concepts.significance: The main path from a Keras model to mobile/embedded inference in the TensorFlow ecosystem.
concepts.example: Running the spam classifier inside an Android chat app.
concepts.misconception: That it trains models. It is an inference runtime.

concepts.name: ONNX / ONNX runtime
concepts.definition: Open Neural Network Exchange, a portable model format, and its runtime.
concepts.intuition: A common file format that many inference engines can read.
concepts.technical: Keras `export()` can produce an ONNX save; the ONNX runtime runs on servers, mobile devices and (p.211) in JavaScript.
concepts.example: Exporting a Keras model to ONNX and running it in a C++ or mobile app.
concepts.misconception: That ONNX is tied to one framework. It is a cross-framework standard.

deeper.title: A quick decision procedure for deployment targets
deeper.body:
Combining p.209–p.211 into a checklist (our synthesis):

1. **Must the data stay on the user's device?** (end-to-end encryption, strict privacy) → device or browser.
2. **Is there a hard latency budget well under ~500 ms, or no reliable connection?** → device or browser.
3. **Can the model be shrunk to fit memory/power, and is some accuracy loss acceptable?** If not, you may have to revisit the requirements.
4. **Otherwise** → REST API, then decide between self-hosting and a managed service like Cloud AI Platform.

deeper.title: Why batching matters for managed servers
deeper.body: Beyond the book: GPUs are throughput machines. Running one input at a time leaves most of the hardware idle. Serving systems therefore collect requests that arrive within a short window (a few ms) into a single batch. This raises throughput a lot at the cost of a small extra latency, and managed platforms tune the tradeoff for you.

deeper.title: How models are made small enough
deeper.body: Beyond the book: common techniques are **post-training quantization** (storing weights as int8 instead of float32 cuts size by 4×), **pruning** (removing near-zero weights), **knowledge distillation** (training a small model to mimic a big one), and **efficient architectures** such as depthwise separable convolutions. Lower-precision computation is covered later in the book (chapter 18, around p.580).

deeper.title: Analogy: restaurant vs. home cooking
deeper.body: REST serving is a restaurant: a big professional kitchen (GPU server), but you must travel there (network) and the chef sees your order (data). On-device inference is cooking at home: a smaller kitchen with simpler dishes (smaller model), but instant, private and possible during a storm (offline).

misconceptions.claim: Deploying on a device always means using a weak, tiny processor.
misconceptions.correction: The book's cookie detector runs at the factory on a GPU. Device deployment means the model runs locally, not necessarily on constrained hardware.

misconceptions.claim: SSL encryption of HTTP requests makes server-side inference acceptable for any sensitive data.
misconceptions.correction: SSL protects data in transit, but the server must decrypt it so the model can read it. For end-to-end encrypted data such as the spam app's messages, the model must run on the device.

misconceptions.claim: You need a separate export path for mobile.
misconceptions.correction: The same `export()` method produces a TensorFlow or ONNX save. TensorFlow Lite uses the same saved-model format as TensorFlow Serving.

misconceptions.claim: The deployed edge model will match the best validation accuracy you achieved.
misconceptions.correction: Memory and power constraints often force shipping a model that isn't quite as good as the best one you could run on a large GPU.

takeaways: Image search, music recommendation, fraud detection and satellite imagery are all good fits for REST serving.
REST serving can be self-hosted or managed; managed services like Cloud AI Platform handle batching, load balancing and scaling.
Deploy on device when latency or connectivity is critical, the model can be made small, peak accuracy is not mission critical, or data must not be decrypted remotely.
Efficiency and accuracy trade off: device constraints often mean shipping a less accurate model.
The spam filter goes on-device for privacy; the cookie detector goes on-site for latency, and it can still use a GPU.
export() produces TensorFlow or ONNX saves; TensorFlow Lite and the ONNX runtime run them on phones and embedded hardware.

questions.question: Which project from chapter 6 must run on the end user's smartphone, and why?
options: The music recommender, because recommendations must be instant
The spam detector, because messages are end-to-end encrypted
The satellite imagery project, because images are large
The fraud detector, because transactions are sensitive
questions.answer: The spam detector, because messages are end-to-end encrypted
questions.explanation: The page states that the spam model must run on the phone because end-to-end encrypted messages cannot be read by a remote model. The book lists the recommender, satellite and fraud projects as good REST API fits.

questions.question: Name three practical details that a managed service such as Cloud AI Platform takes care of.
questions.answer: Batching predictions, load balancing, and scaling.
questions.explanation: These are listed explicitly in the paragraph on self-hosting vs. managed services.

questions.question: Why does the bad-cookie detector run 'on device', and how does its situation differ from the usual image of on-device ML?
questions.answer: It has strict latency constraints, so it must run at the factory. Unlike phones or microcontrollers, there are no power or space constraints there, so it can run on a GPU.
questions.explanation: The book shows that device deployment is about location and latency, not necessarily weak hardware.

questions.question: Which statement about TensorFlow Lite is correct according to the page?
options: It requires a different model format from TensorFlow Serving
It uses the same TensorFlow save model format as TensorFlow Serving
It is used to train models on microcontrollers
questions.answer: It uses the same TensorFlow save model format as TensorFlow Serving
questions.explanation: The page says this explicitly. TF Lite also runs on iOS, ARM CPUs, Raspberry Pi and certain microcontrollers, and it is an inference framework, not a training framework.

questions.question: Explain the efficiency/accuracy tradeoff mentioned for on-device deployment and what it implies for stakeholder communication.
questions.answer: Memory and power limits force smaller models, which are usually less accurate than the best model on a large GPU. Stakeholders should therefore expect the deployed model to fall somewhat short of the best results seen in development.
questions.explanation: This combines the third bullet with section 6.3.1 on setting expectations (p.208).

questions.question: Give the four conditions under which the book recommends deploying on a device.
questions.answer: (1) Strict latency constraints or a low-connectivity environment; (2) the model can be made small enough for the device's memory/power; (3) highest accuracy is not mission critical; (4) the input data is strictly sensitive and shouldn't be decryptable on a remote server.
questions.explanation: These are the four bullets on the page.

questions.question: For an AR glasses app that labels objects in real time, could you use a REST API? Justify using the page's criteria.
questions.answer: No. The book notes that querying a remote server is not viable for immersive AR because of latency (a REST round trip takes about 500 ms, p.209). The model must run on the device.
questions.explanation: This applies the first bullet, which uses AR as its example.
